reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a one-click tenfold-profit bot, instructs viewers to deploy and fund a contract with BNB, and activate automated trades. It claims that 90% of profits return to the wallet and that more capital could produce over a thousand BNB per day. Although educational and risk disclaimers are present, they do not remove the video's concrete funding instructions and unusually large return claims.

opening.argument: Judge, the title's profit claim should be read alongside the video's explicit warnings, not as a promise to viewers. The description says, "Use at your own risk," calls cryptocurrency a "very high-risk investment," and states that the speaker "does not guarantee any particular outcome." It also explains that fees and token burns can consume the amount available to trade. Those qualifications are unusually concrete: they give viewers reasons the demonstrated approach might lose money or fail to produce the advertised result. The evidence supports a risky trading tutorial with aggressive promotional language, but does not establish that the creator assures viewers of a return.

citations.quote: Use at your own risk.
Cryptocurrency is HIGHLY volatile and a very high-risk investment.
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.
I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited directions to fund a contract and press its action button establish what the tutorial demonstrates, not that the creator guarantees the depicted returns. Even the amount is introduced as "For the sake of this video," while the description expressly warns of substantial loss and disclaims any guaranteed outcome. The opening treats instructions plus an ambitious claim as sufficient, without addressing those qualifications.

citations.quote: For the sake of this video 0.2 BNB. Might as well make it a 0.4.
Trading cryptocurrencies poses considerable risk of loss.
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A non-guarantee disclaimer does not undo the pitch. The title promises "Auto x10 Profit With One Click," and the speaker directs viewers to fund the contract, activate it, and expect money back within minutes. The warnings describe trading risk but do not substantiate the claimed automated returns or change the concrete invitation to put BNB into the promoted contract.

opening.argument: Judge, the substance is a walkthrough of a smart-contract workflow. The speaker identifies Remix, creates a contract, discusses the wrapped BNB address and PancakeSwap router, then compiles and deploys it. The description explicitly calls this "a simple front run deployment in Solidity." The sampled screen also shows the Remix development interface. Funding and activating the contract are steps in that demonstration; their presence does not alone turn instruction about a tool into a solicitation. The speaker's reported profit is a claim about personal experience, not independent proof of the contract's performance, but the central material remains a technical demonstration.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening accurately identifies deployment, funding, and activation, but those are also the operations needed to demonstrate the contract the speaker is explaining. It does not show that the claimed trades or returns were independently verified. The speaker even presents the BscScan report as something he "can show," rather than supplying corroboration in that statement. A demonstration can contain an overstated result without its instructional subject ceasing to be central.

which I can show the. Transaction or report from BSC scan to corroborate that.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is the mechanism of the pitch, not merely background education. The speaker tells viewers to copy contract information from the description, fund the deployed contract, and press an action button said to trade automatically. He then claims it is "already around 50x." Technical steps do not neutralize an invitation to send BNB into a contract on the strength of extraordinary return claims.

opening.argument: Judge, the described transaction is a user operating a trading contract, not an identified payment to the creator. The speaker says to deploy it "to our wallet," send funds to "that contract that we just created," and use an action function said to return proceeds to the wallet. The description points to MetaMask and Remix as tools for that workflow. Nothing in those cited steps identifies a creator-controlled recipient, asks for wallet credentials, or describes referral income. Those absences cannot prove the code is safe; they do matter when deciding whether the supplied evidence establishes a deceptive transfer scheme rather than a risky, possibly exaggerated bot tutorial.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening calls funding itself incriminating, but its cited wording says "funding your contract," not sending money to a named seller or paying for access. The action button is described as engaging the PancakeSwap router. Neither point establishes who ultimately controls the contract's funds or whether the promised automation works. The large earnings claim warrants skepticism, but the cited workflow alone does not resolve those questions.

citations.quote: the next step in this process is just funding your contract
The action button then engages all the constructors that I built in as far as engaging the pancake. Router.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a named recipient or credential request does not make a funded-contract pitch ordinary instruction. Viewers are directed to paste the supplied contract, fund it, and activate it, while the title advertises tenfold profit and the speaker suggests a thousand BNB a day with more capital. The supplied material does not verify that the code sends profits back as claimed; a wallet-based workflow can still expose the deposited BNB to the promoted contract.
